title: Outdoor coil sensor open / shorted
shortDescription: Outdoor coil thermistor read out of range, blocking proper defrost control.
fullDescription:
Nordyne heat pumps (also sold as Maytag, Frigidaire, Westinghouse, Tappan) use an outdoor coil thermistor to time defrost cycles. E1 reports the sensor as open, shorted, or showing physically impossible values. Without this sensor the system either skips defrost or gets stuck in defrost.

The sensor is a 10K NTC clipped to a return-bend on the lower outdoor coil. Common failures: vibration breaks the lead at the strain relief, or rodents chew the cable.
safetyWarning: Lock out the disconnect at the heat pump before opening the panel. 240 VAC is present at the contactor.

fixSteps.title: Power off + verify zero volts
fixSteps.instruction: Pull disconnect; verify L1-L2 reads 0 V at contactor.

fixSteps.title: Locate and inspect sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Find the small thermistor clipped to a coil U-bend. Check leads for breaks.

fixSteps.title: Resistance check
fixSteps.instruction: Compare to OEM chart - 10K at 77 F is typical. Replace if open.

whenToCallPro: If sensor checks good, the control board input is suspect.

faq.q: Can I run without the sensor?
faq.a: The system uses time-based defrost as a fallback but efficiency suffers.

title: Outdoor ambient sensor fault
shortDescription: Ambient air thermistor open or out of range.
fullDescription:
E2 indicates the outdoor ambient temperature thermistor failed, is shorted, or is reporting a value outside the physically possible window. The board uses ambient temperature for low-temperature lockouts and to manage variable-speed compressor capacity.

With E2 active, low-temperature heat-pump operation is locked out and electric strip heat takes over - this can cause shockingly high electric bills.
safetyWarning: 240 VAC present in the outdoor unit. Verify zero volts before service.

fixSteps.title: Identify ambient sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Sensor is mounted in airflow path with a wire pigtail to the control board.

fixSteps.title: Resistance test
fixSteps.instruction: Should match 10K chart at outdoor temp. Replace if open or wildly off.

whenToCallPro: If new sensor still produces E2, control board failure.

faq.q: Why is my electric bill so high with E2?
faq.a: Heat pump won't run; resistance heat carries the entire load at 3-4x the cost.

title: High pressure switch open
shortDescription: Discharge pressure exceeded the safety cutout (~600 psi R-410A).
fullDescription:
E3 means the high-pressure switch opened. Compressor stops to prevent rupture. On heat pumps in heating mode, common causes are an iced indoor coil with reduced airflow, dirty filter, restricted ductwork, or failure of the indoor blower. In cooling mode, dirty outdoor coil and failed condenser fan top the list.

In heat-pump heating: a stuck reversing valve can also send hot gas the wrong direction and cause this code.
safetyWarning: Refrigerant work requires EPA 608 certification. High-pressure refrigerant can cause severe injury.

fixSteps.title: Replace indoor filter
fixSteps.instruction: Restore airflow over the indoor coil immediately.

fixSteps.title: Wash outdoor coil
fixSteps.instruction: With power off, gently rinse from inside out.

fixSteps.title: Verify both fans run
fixSteps.instruction: On a call, both indoor blower and outdoor fan should run.

fixSteps.title: Tech pressure check
fixSteps.instruction: Have refrigerant pressures and subcool/superheat verified.

whenToCallPro: Refrigerant adjustment, valve replacement, fan motor replacement.

faq.q: Why does the heat pump trip in heating mode?
faq.a: In heating, the indoor coil is the condenser. Restricted indoor airflow raises high-side pressure dramatically.

title: Low pressure / loss of charge
shortDescription: Suction pressure below cutout - leak, restriction, or low-temperature operation.
fullDescription:
E4 indicates the low-pressure switch opened (typically below 50 psi R-410A) or the system inferred low charge from sensor data. The compressor stops to prevent damage from liquid floodback or starved lubrication.

Most common: refrigerant leak in evaporator, line set, or service valve cores. Operation below 30 F outdoors without low-ambient kit can also trigger E4 transiently.
safetyWarning: Refrigerant repairs are EPA 608 only. Ventilate confined spaces - refrigerant displaces oxygen.

fixSteps.title: Replace filter, thaw coil
fixSteps.instruction: Run blower-only for 1-2 hours to thaw any indoor coil ice.

fixSteps.title: Verify service valves open
fixSteps.instruction: Both stem caps off and valves back-seated.

fixSteps.title: Tech leak search and repair
fixSteps.instruction: Electronic detector, dye, then repair / pull vacuum / weigh in.

faq.a: EPA prohibits topping off without leak repair, and the leak will return.

title: Compressor over-current
shortDescription: Compressor drew current above the safety threshold.
fullDescription:
E5 means the compressor exceeded its rated running or starting current. Causes include a failed run capacitor, low line voltage, overcharge, or seizing windings.

On variable-capacity Nordyne (iQ Drive) units, the inverter detects this directly. On single-stage units it's an external thermal overload.
safetyWarning: Capacitors hold lethal charge after disconnect. Discharge through a 20 K-ohm resistor before testing.

fixSteps.title: Discharge and test capacitor
fixSteps.instruction: After power-off, short cap terminals through resistor, measure uF.

fixSteps.title: Verify line voltage under load
fixSteps.instruction: Should stay above 207 VAC during start.

fixSteps.title: Inspect contactor
fixSteps.instruction: Look for pitting and welded contacts.

title: Reversing valve fault
shortDescription: Reversing valve failed to shift between heating and cooling modes.
fullDescription:
E6 indicates the system commanded a mode change but the discharge / suction temperature pattern shows the valve did not shift. The slide can stick mid-stroke after long idle periods, or the solenoid coil can fail open.

A single full cycle of cool-then-heat sometimes frees a mildly stuck valve. Persistent E6 means valve replacement.
safetyWarning: Reversing valve replacement requires EPA 608 recovery and brazing.

fixSteps.title: Test solenoid coil
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect plug; ohm coil. Open = replace coil only.

fixSteps.title: Force a mode swap
fixSteps.instruction: Alternate cooling and heating from thermostat to free a slightly stuck slide.

fixSteps.title: Tech replacement
fixSteps.instruction: Recover, replace valve body, evacuate, weigh in charge.

faq.q: Why does my heat pump blow cold air on heat call?
faq.a: Reversing valve didn't shift - that's E6.

title: Defrost stuck active
shortDescription: System exceeded the maximum defrost time without exiting defrost mode.
fullDescription:
E7 means the heat pump entered defrost but never reached the temperature or pressure target to exit. Maximum defrost time (typically 10 minutes) elapsed and the board flagged the fault.

Causes: failed coil sensor, severe ice buildup, drain pan ice covering the lower coil, failed reversing valve, low refrigerant charge.
safetyWarning: Coil ice in extreme cold can damage the lower coil and pan. Do not chip ice with metal tools.

fixSteps.title: Power off + thaw
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect power; allow ice to melt naturally. Pour warm water carefully if needed - never hot.

fixSteps.title: Verify drain
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm the base pan drain hole is clear.

faq.q: Should I pour hot water on the coil?
faq.a: Use warm water only - boiling water can crack copper return bends.

title: Discharge line over-temperature
shortDescription: Compressor discharge thermistor exceeded safety threshold (typically 270 F).
fullDescription:
E8 indicates excess discharge temperature - dangerous to the compressor and refrigerant oil. System pauses 5 minutes then retries.

Causes include low charge, restricted liquid line, dirty coils, or failed compressor valves.
safetyWarning: Refrigerant lines can cause severe burns. Allow to cool 30 minutes before touching.

fixSteps.title: Wash outdoor coil
fixSteps.instruction: Power off; rinse from inside out.

title: Inverter / drive fault (iQ Drive)
shortDescription: Variable-speed drive reported internal fault: IGBT, DC bus, or output ground fault.
fullDescription:
E9 is a generic drive fault on Nordyne iQ Drive variable-capacity heat pumps. Drive is sealed and replaced as a unit.

Before replacing, verify clean drive heatsink, tight power lugs, and good line filter. Compressor windings should be checked for short to ground.
safetyWarning: DC bus capacitors hold lethal charge for 5+ minutes. Verify zero volts before service.

causes.cause: Loose lug or burned line filter

fixSteps.title: Power off + 5 min wait
fixSteps.instruction: Verify zero V at DC bus before service.

fixSteps.title: Clean heatsink
fixSteps.instruction: Vacuum dust; verify drive cooling fan operation.

fixSteps.title: Tech drive replacement
fixSteps.instruction: Sealed drive replaced as a unit.

faq.a: Most iQ Drive units carry 10-year parts warranty when registered.

title: Communication loss with indoor unit
shortDescription: Communication bus between outdoor unit and air handler dropped.
fullDescription:
E10 indicates loss of the proprietary communication packets between outdoor heat pump and indoor air handler / furnace. Common after wiring repair, voltage spike, or rodent damage.

Verify polarity (i+ to i+), check for water in outdoor whip, and confirm 24 V transformer fuse is intact.
safetyWarning: Low-voltage but a shorted comm wire can blow the transformer fuse.
symptoms: System runs at default fixed capacity

fixSteps.title: Verify polarity
fixSteps.instruction: i+ to i+ at both ends; not swapped.

fixSteps.title: Inspect whip
fixSteps.instruction: Open outdoor whip, check for moisture, corrosion.

fixSteps.title: Continuity test cable
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect both ends; verify no shorts and full continuity.

whenToCallPro: If thermostat cable replacement is needed.

faq.a: Yes, on default fixed-capacity logic - efficiency suffers.
